title: PittyTiger
summary: PittyTiger is an intrusion set that public reporting described in 2013 after a series of attacks against Indian government and military related organisations. The tradecraft was simple and cheap: spear phishing email with documents that exploited old, well known flaws in office and document reader software, followed by widely available remote access tools rather than custom malware. Because the tooling was commodity, the group's activity was easy to confuse with criminal opportunism, and later analysis noted that some of the same tools were used by several unrelated actors. That overlap is the main lesson of the case: reuse of public tools weakens both attribution and signature-based detection, so defenders should focus on behaviour such as the process chain that follows a document being opened rather than on malware names. Evidence in an environment is a document that spawns a script or a system utility, a newly created auto-start entry, and periodic outbound connections to commodity hosting. Public reporting has not established a convincing sponsor, and the group's name reflects a word found in its tooling rather than a confirmed organisation.

beginner.definition: PittyTiger is the name for a group of attackers who targeted government offices in India around 2013. Researchers named them after a word found in their software. They used cheap, publicly available tools instead of building their own, and nobody has proved who was behind them.
beginner.whyItMatters: Not every attacker writes new software. Many buy or download tools that thousands of other people already use. This makes them cheap and fast, but it also makes them hard to identify. If your defences only look for known bad programs, these attackers slip past, so watching behaviour works much better.
howItWorks: The attackers send email with an attached document to staff in government offices.
The document uses an old software flaw to run code when a user opens it.
The code downloads a remote control program from a public file sharing site.
The program copies itself somewhere unusual and sets itself to start automatically.
The operator then browses files, reads documents and looks for other computers.
They often stop after a short time and return later with a new tool.
beginner.example: Imagine a burglar who buys the same lock picking set as everyone else. The police cannot tell which burglar visited, because the marks on the door all look the same. Two different burglars would leave the same traces, so the report cannot name one of them. Only behaviour gives a clue, such as the time of night, the room chosen and the way the window was left. The tools themselves tell the investigator almost nothing.
takeaways: Commodity attack tools are common and cheap, so behaviour matters more than names.
An old document reader flaw can still be the first step of an intrusion.
When attribution is unclear, say so instead of guessing who did it.

objectives: Explain why groups that use commodity tools are difficult to attribute.
Describe how a document exploit leads to a downloaded remote access tool.
Explain the value of behaviour-based detection over signature matching.
Identify the auto-start and process artefacts left by commodity malware.
Explain how to report attribution honestly when the evidence is weak.
